summary: Silent Sentinels is an interactive web experience that transforms NASA's abandoned hardware on the Moon and Mars into compelling stories of exploration and discovery. We developed a feature-rich webapp that includes an interactive planetary atlas where users can toggle between the Moon and Mars, explore every landing site with mission pins, and scrub through a timeline spanning sixty years of space exploration (1966–2026). Each mission is brought to life through an illustrated graphic novel with ten comic pages, alongside detailed mission dossiers featuring real telemetry and instrument data. The project directly addresses the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge by reframing discarded equipment — rovers, landers, and scientific instruments — not as space junk, but as eternal monuments of human curiosity. Designed for students in grades 4–12, Silent Sentinels makes space archaeology accessible and inspiring, encouraging the next generation to see these silent pioneers as proof that exploration never truly ends.
details:
What It Does

Silent Sentinels is an interactive web experience that reimagines NASA's abandoned hardware on the Moon and Mars as enduring monuments of human exploration. Instead of treating discarded rovers, landers, and instruments as forgotten space junk, our project brings each piece of equipment back to life through immersive storytelling and interactive data visualization.

How It Works

The webapp features three core modules:

  • Interactive Planetary Atlas — Users explore a satellite-imagery basemap sourced from NASA Solar System Treks, toggle between the Moon and Mars, and pinpoint every historical landing site with mission markers. A timeline scrubber lets users travel through sixty years of missions (1966–2026), with quick-jump buttons for major milestones like Apollo 11, Viking 1, and InSight.
  • Graphic Novel & Mission Dossiers — An orbital arc selector showcases five iconic missions: Surveyor 3, Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Viking 1, Opportunity, and InSight. Each mission offers a ten-page illustrated comic that narrates its story in an engaging, visual format, alongside a Mission Dossier view with real telemetry data and instrument details.
  • Space Archaeology & STEM Education Hub — Informational cards explain why this hardware matters as protected heritage, what scientific breakthroughs these instruments enabled, and how they inspire future explorers. An FAQ section addresses common questions about why NASA leaves hardware behind and which instruments still function today.

Benefits & Intended Impact

The project makes space history accessible and exciting for students in grades 4–12. By combining interactive maps, comic-style storytelling, and real mission data, it bridges the gap between raw NASA datasets and engaging educational content. Our goal is to spark curiosity in robotics, astrophysics, and space engineering among young learners.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (interactive atlas, animations, comic reader)
  • Design: Deep-space sci-fi aesthetic with glassmorphic UI, animated starfields, neon teal accents, and monospace typography
  • Data Sources: NASA Solar System Treks, Planetary Data System (PDS), Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, data.nasa.gov
  • AI Tools: Antigravity (webapp code generation and development), ChatGPT & Claude (ideation, prompt crafting, and content structuring)
  • Deployment: Vercel

What Makes It Creative

Rather than building a static informational page, we designed Silent Sentinels as an experience — users "pull away from Earth" as they scroll, journey through decades on a timeline, and read illustrated comics that humanize robotic missions. The graphic novel format is unconventional for a data-driven challenge and makes complex mission histories digestible for younger audiences.

Team Considerations

We prioritized accessibility for our target age group (grades 4–12), ensuring the language is approachable, the navigation is intuitive, and the visuals are captivating enough to hold attention. We also ensured all mission data is sourced from official NASA archives for scientific accuracy.
